concepts.title: Cell Signaling: Paracrine Autocrine and Endocrine

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cell Signaling: Paracrine Autocrine and Endocrine' refers to.
questions.a: Cells converse through chemical messengers that only work where a matching receptor waits: short-range release reaching neighbours at once is paracrine, a cell talking back to its own receptors is autocrine - the trick cancer cells abuse by making their own growth factors - and hormones riding the bloodstream to distant targets is endocrine signaling.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cell Signaling: Paracrine Autocrine and Endocrine'.
questions.a: Distance decides the name of the signaling; no receptor on the cell means no response, whatever the ligand level.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cell Signaling: Paracrine Autocrine and Endocrine' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Glycolysis and the Fate of Pyruvate

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Glycolysis and the Fate of Pyruvate' refers to.
questions.a: In the cytosol the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas route splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates over ten enzyme steps, spending two ATP early and banking four later, with hexokinase, phosphofructokinase and pyruvate kinase marking the three irreversible control points; afterwards pyruvate either becomes lactate or ethanol without air, or enters mitochondria as acetyl CoA when oxygen is present.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Glycolysis and the Fate of Pyruvate'.
questions.a: Three regulated, irreversible enzymes steer glycolysis, and oxygen availability alone picks pyruvate's next destination.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Glycolysis and the Fate of Pyruvate' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Citric Acid Cycle in the Mitochondrial Matrix

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Citric Acid Cycle in the Mitochondrial Matrix' refers to.
questions.a: Hans Kreb's cycle condenses a two-carbon acetyl group with four-carbon oxaloacetate into citrate and walks it through decarboxylations and dehydrogenations back to oxaloacetate, banking three NADH, one FADH2 and one GTP per turn; all its enzymes sit in the mitochondrial matrix except succinate dehydrogenase, which alone is embedded in the inner membrane.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Citric Acid Cycle in the Mitochondrial Matrix'.
questions.a: One turn burns one acetyl group to two CO2 while loading three NADH, one FADH2 and one GTP.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Citric Acid Cycle in the Mitochondrial Matrix' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Meiosis, Apoptosis, Stem Cells and Migration

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meiosis, Apoptosis, Stem Cells and Migration' refers to.
questions.a: Two reductions shape cell life: meiosis halves the chromosome set across a reductional first division and an equational second one, delivering four haploid cells enriched by crossing over at pachytene; apoptosis then prunes unneeded cells by programmed DNA fragmentation and membrane blebbing without inflammation, unlike traumatic necrosis; meanwhile stem cells of totipotent, pluripotent or multipotent grade repair tissues, and cell migration walks single cells or sheets through embryogenesis, wound healing and cancer spread.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meiosis, Apoptosis, Stem Cells and Migration'.
questions.a: Halving, pruning, specialising and moving - the four long-term acts that shape a multicellular organism.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meiosis, Apoptosis, Stem Cells and Migration' taught, and from which source text?
